state.misconception_label: Believes f(x - a) translates the function up a units

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: What transformation maps the graph of \(y=f(x) \) to the graph of \( y=f(x-3) \). I got Translation by vector
\(
\left[\begin{array}{l}
0 \\
3
\end{array}\right]
\) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: It seems like you may be interpreting the transformation as moving the graph up by 3 units. Let's focus on how the transformation affects the x-values in the function. Can you think about how changing the input in f(x) to f(x-3) impacts the graph?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I think I get what you're saying about how it changes the x-values. So, if I change \(x\) to \(x-3\), it kind of moves the graph to the right instead of up? But I'm still a bit confused about how that works exactly. Can you explain why it moves right and not up?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: That's a great observation! When you substitute \(x-3\) for \(x\) in the function, it shifts the graph horizontally by 3 units to the right, not up. Think about how this change affects the x-values and how that translates into the graph's movement. Can you see how adjusting the input value impacts the location of the graph?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I think I'm starting to understand it better! So, when I put \(x-3\) in the function, it makes the x-values bigger, which moves the graph to the right. But why does it work that way? Like, why does subtracting 3 from \(x\) mean I have to go right instead of left?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher correctly identifies and addresses the specific misconception about vertical vs. horizontal translation, but relies heavily on telling rather than eliciting reasoning, and the student's final turn reveals persistent confusion about why the transformation works as it does.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher breaks down the problem and provides some scaffolding by directing attention to x-values, they repeatedly tell the student the answer (that it shifts right by 3 units) rather than using questions or smaller steps to help the student construct this understanding themselves.
